edits.before: A clause with one variable has a forced value which can be replaced in all other equations or considered to be a clause with the same variable twice. Regardless it need not effect the implication graph or could be a trivial self-loop.

edits.before_tex: A clause with one variable has a forced value which can be replaced in all other equations or considered to be a clause with the same variable twice.  Regardless it need not effect the implication graph or could be a trivial self-loop.
edits.after: A clause with one literal l has a forced value which can be substituted into all other clauses, or the clause can be considered to be (l or l), which yields the single implication (not l) implies l. In the second case the implication is an edge of the implication graph (from the negation of the literal to the literal), not a self-loop, and it must not be dropped: omitting it would make (x) and (not x) together appear satisfiable.
edits.after_tex: A clause with one variable has a forced value which can be substituted into all other equations, or considered to be a clause with the same literal twice, $(\ell\vee\ell)$, which yields the single implication $\lnot\ell\implies\ell$.  In the second case this is an edge of the implication graph (from $\lnot\ell$ to $\ell$), not a self-loop, and it cannot be omitted: otherwise $(x)\wedge(\lnot x)$ would appear satisfiable.
edits.reason: For (l or l) the two contrapositive implications coincide in the single edge (not l) -> l, which is not a self-loop and carries the constraint; the published sentence says it is unnecessary or trivial.
edits.evidence: Derived from the clause/implication definition of the same paragraph; the repository gettwosatgraph encodes the unit clause as the edge (not x) -> x; Lean statement in R5.
